newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin and top ministers discuss reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin and top ministers discuss reforms.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin met top members of his government on Tuesday to discuss the course of their economic reforms, the Kremlin said.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and his two first deputies, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, took part in the meeting along with Valentin Yumashev, who heads Yeltsin's administration, Russian news agencies reported.
Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said on Monday the meeting would review the government's record in the first six months of the year.

The agencies said Yeltsin had opened the meeting with a question over the situation in the troubled Far Eastern region, where about 300 employees of the Zvezda nuclear submarine servicing plant broke through police barriers and blocked the Trans-Siberian railway for about two hours on Tuesday.
Police in riot gear tried to prevent the workers, who say they have not been paid for 10 months, from blocking the tracks.
Reuters Television showed protesters squeezing through police ranks but there were no large-scale clashes.
Protesters had said they were determined to stay on the tracks until they receive tens of billions of roubles (millions of dollars) in back wages.
The Russian news agencies did not give other details of the start of the session conducted by Yeltsin at a state residence in Moscow, the rest of which was held behind closed doors.
Yeltsin reshuffled the government dramatically in March, putting reformers like Chubais, 41, and Nemtsov, 37, into key posts to reinvigorate market reforms under the veteran but loyal Chernomyrdin.
He had called the previous cabinet "stagnant" and gave the new one strong support in its efforts to put state finances in order, reorganise natural monopolies and fight corruption.

The government says it has met Yeltsin's demands and paid off a huge backlog of pensions by Tuesday. Chernomyrdin said on Monday the next priority would be the armed forces, where discontent is rife over non-payment of salaries and general decline.

One of the issues likely to emerge at the meeting on Tuesday was resistance from the opposition-dominated State Duma, the lower house of parliament, to a package of market reform legislation proposed by the cabinet.

The Duma went on holiday last week until September 1 after rejecting cabinet proposals to cut 1997 budget spending across the board because of revenue shortfalls, and to slash some social benefits -- a legacy of Soviet paternalism the government says it can no longer afford.
Yeltsin and Chubais, both known for a tough line towards the Duma, have said the government will pursue its policy regardless of whether it has the legislature's backing.

But Chernomyrdin took a slightly more conciliatory line on Monday, saying the cabinet needed the Duma's support and promising to try to persuade deputies to interrupt their holiday and consider the most pressing draft bills in July.

The head of the Duma, Gennady Seleznyov, told reporters after meeting faction leaders that convening a special session might be possible, but only if the government revised its original plans -- a clear reference to the Duma's earlier requests that spending cuts, known as sequestration, be limited.

"Our common opinion is that it only makes sense to meet if we see the sequestration law in a new wording which is close to recommendations from that part of the conciliatory commission which represented the Duma," he said.
"It is pointless to meet if we see the version which the government has already advocated."
Chernomyrdin was expected to meet Seleznyov on Tuesday to discuss the situation.
